guide.title: Period 5 (1844–1877): review guide
guide.intro: Expansion across the continent reopened the question of slavery in new territories. Compromise failed, the Union split and fought a civil war, and Reconstruction tried, and in many ways failed, to secure the rights of freed people.

sections.title: Manifest Destiny and the Mexican–American War
body: Manifest Destiny held that the United States was destined to spread across the continent. The United States annexed Texas (1845), divided Oregon with Britain (1846), and won the Mexican–American War (1846–1848), gaining California and much of the Southwest in the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo.

Expansion displaced American Indians and Mexican residents and made the status of slavery in the new lands the central political question, starting with the Wilmot Proviso (1846), which proposed banning slavery in land taken from Mexico.
points: Contextualization: expansion was driven by land hunger, economic opportunity, and ideas of destiny.
The Mexican Cession reopened the slavery question.

sections.title: Sectional conflict and secession
body: The Compromise of 1850 admitted California as a free state and passed a stronger Fugitive Slave Act, which angered many Northerners. The Kansas–Nebraska Act (1854) let settlers decide on slavery (popular sovereignty), leading to violence in Kansas and the rise of the Republican Party, which opposed slavery's expansion.

The Dred Scott decision (1857) ruled that Black people could not be citizens and that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories. After Abraham Lincoln won the election of 1860 without Southern electoral votes, seven Deep South states seceded before his inauguration.
points: Each compromise solved one problem and created new conflict.
Republicans opposed slavery's spread, not (at first) slavery where it existed.

sections.title: The Civil War and Reconstruction
body: The Union's industrial and population advantages, the naval blockade, and eventually the Emancipation Proclamation (1863) and Black soldiers' service helped it win. War aims shifted from preserving the Union to ending slavery. Wartime laws such as the Homestead Act and Pacific Railway Act reshaped the West.

Reconstruction brought the Thirteenth (abolishing slavery), Fourteenth (citizenship and equal protection), and Fifteenth (voting regardless of race) Amendments. Freed people built schools, churches, and families and held office, but Black Codes, Klan violence, Northern weariness, and the Compromise of 1877 ended federal protection, and Southern states later denied Black citizens their rights.
points: Comparison: Reconstruction's goals vs. its results.
The amendments later provided the legal basis for the civil rights movement.

example.prompt: Explain one way the Mexican–American War increased sectional conflict.
example.solution: The war added vast territory, and Congress then had to decide whether slavery would be allowed there. Proposals such as the Wilmot Proviso, which would have banned slavery in the Mexican Cession, divided Northern and Southern members along sectional lines.

misconceptions: “The Civil War was fought to end slavery from the start.”
Lincoln's first aim was preserving the Union; emancipation became a war aim in 1862–1863.
“The Emancipation Proclamation freed all enslaved people.”
It applied to Confederate-held areas; the Thirteenth Amendment ended slavery nationwide.
It produced lasting constitutional amendments, though protection of rights collapsed.
“Republicans in 1860 wanted to abolish slavery everywhere.”
Their platform opposed its expansion into the territories.

passages.title: Source A: Abraham Lincoln, letter to Horace Greeley, 1862
text: “I would save the Union. I would save it the shortest way under the Constitution. . . . My paramount object in this struggle is to save the Union, and is not either to save or destroy Slavery. If I could save the Union without freeing any slave, I would do it, and if I could save it by freeing all the slaves, I would do it, and if I could save it by freeing some and leaving others alone, I would also do that. . . . I have here stated my purpose according to my view of official duty, and I intend no modification of my oft-expressed personal wish that all men, everywhere, could be free.”
passages.attribution: President Abraham Lincoln, public letter to newspaper editor Horace Greeley, August 22, 1862. Public domain. Wording follows the excerpt quoted in OpenStax U.S. History, section 15.3.
passages.licenseOrRights: The original text is in the public domain (published before 1931, or a work of the U.S. government). StudySprint quotes it as excerpted in OpenStax U.S. History (openstax.org/books/us-history/pages/15-3-1863-the-changing-nature-of-the-war); no OpenStax commentary is copied.

passages.title: Source B: Testimony of Abram Colby to Congress, 1871
text: “On the 29th of October, they came to my house and broke my door open, took me out of my bed and took me to the woods and whipped me three hours or more and left me in the woods for dead. They said to me, “Do you think you will ever vote another damned Radical ticket?” . . . I said, “If there was an election to-morrow, I would vote the Radical ticket.” They set in and whipped me a thousand licks more, I suppose. . . . They said I had influence with the negroes of other counties, and had carried the negroes against them.”
passages.attribution: Abram Colby, a formerly enslaved man elected to the Georgia legislature in 1868, testifying on October 27, 1871, to the congressional joint committee investigating the Ku Klux Klan (published 1872). Public domain. Wording follows the excerpt quoted in OpenStax U.S. History, section 16.4.
passages.licenseOrRights: The original text is in the public domain (published before 1931, or a work of the U.S. government). StudySprint quotes it as excerpted in OpenStax U.S. History (openstax.org/books/us-history/pages/16-4-the-collapse-of-reconstruction); no OpenStax commentary is copied.

passages.title: Source C: An interpretation of Manifest Destiny
text: “Americans of the 1840s spoke of their expansion as natural and even divinely ordained. But the territory gained between 1845 and 1848 came through annexation, negotiation, and a war with Mexico that many Americans at the time, including a young congressman named Abraham Lincoln, opposed. The new lands were home to Mexican citizens and many American Indian nations, and they raised a question that no amount of destiny could answer: would slavery be allowed to spread into them? Expansion did not unite the nation; it set its sections on a collision course.”
passages.attribution: Interpretation written for StudySprint by its editors. It summarizes widely held historical views and is not a quotation from any published historian.
passages.licenseOrRights: Original text written for StudySprint; it is not taken or adapted from any College Board exam.

passages.title: Source D: An interpretation of the failure of compromise in the 1850s
text: “The Compromise of 1850 was meant to settle the slavery question for good. Instead, its Fugitive Slave Act brought slavery into Northern communities, as federal officials pursued people who had escaped, and turned many moderates against the South. Four years later, the Kansas–Nebraska Act undid the Missouri Compromise line and invited settlers to fight over slavery in Kansas. By the time the Supreme Court ruled in Dred Scott that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories, there was little middle ground left.”

preserve the Union

He wants to restore national authority.

questions.prompt: About one month after this letter, Lincoln issued the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation. Which statement best explains how it fit the position in the letter?
choices: It freed enslaved people in the border states that had stayed loyal to the Union in 1861
It was presented as a war measure to help save the Union by weakening the Confederacy
It was required by a Supreme Court ruling on the war powers of the president
It abandoned the goal of preserving the Union in favor of ending slavery
questions.explanation: Lincoln framed emancipation in Confederate-held areas as a military necessity, consistent with saving the Union.
choiceExplanations: It applied to areas in rebellion, not the loyal border states.
No court required it.
Saving the Union remained his aim.

questions.prompt: Lincoln's careful position in the letter is best explained by his need to
choices: persuade Britain to recognize and join the Confederacy in the war
satisfy the Supreme Court, which had ruled in Dred Scott against Congress's powers
win Southern votes in the coming 1860 presidential election
keep the loyal slaveholding border states and Northern moderates behind the war
questions.explanation: Kentucky, Maryland, and Missouri were vital; announcing a war against slavery too early could have pushed them toward the Confederacy.
choiceExplanations: He wanted Britain to stay out of the war.
He wasn't trying to satisfy the Court's Dred Scott ruling.
The 1860 election was already over.

questions.prompt: According to Colby, his attackers were trying to
choices: force him to leave Georgia and move to the North
collect a debt he owed to a local landowner
stop him from supporting the Republican (“Radical”) ticket
recruit him into the Confederate army to fight for the South
questions.explanation: They asked whether he would vote “another damned Radical ticket” and attacked him for influencing other voters.
choiceExplanations: They wanted him to stop his political activity, not move.
Nothing in the testimony suggests a debt.
The war had ended in 1865.

questions.explanation: His account documents Klan violence aimed at Black political participation.

The testimony shows the failure of protection.

the Dred Scott decision of the Supreme Court in 1857
the Compromise of 1850 on slavery in the territories
questions.explanation: Congressional Reconstruction and the Fourteenth Amendment (and soon the Fifteenth) opened politics to Black men.
choiceExplanations: Black Codes restricted freedpeople's rights.
Dred Scott denied Black citizenship.
That compromise concerned slavery in new territories.

questions.explanation: The deal that settled the disputed 1876 election ended military Reconstruction.
choiceExplanations: The Homestead Act (1862) concerned western land.
The proviso was proposed in 1846.
That act was passed in 1854.

choices: prove that Lincoln supported the spread of slavery into the West
explain why Mexico won the war and kept most of its northern lands
show that Congress approved every war the nation fought in the 1840s without debate
show that expansion was contested at the time, not universally accepted
questions.explanation: Pointing to contemporary opponents challenges the idea that expansion was natural and agreed upon.
choiceExplanations: Lincoln's opposition to the war says nothing in favor of slavery.
Mexico lost the war and much of its northern territory.
